questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Colour That Keeps Its Name in Changing Light
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a surface looks the same colour under different illuminants
questions.stem: In an amateur astronomer's log, a red filter looks red at dawn and at dusk; what keeps the name stable across changing light?

options.text: The visual system compares the surface with its surround and preserves its identity
The wavelength of the filter shifts to match the scene
options.misconception: confuses physical change with perceptual stability

options.text: The eye adapts its sensitivity so the same surface keeps one colour name
options.misconception: treats adaptation as a change in the surface itself

options.text: The brain stores a fixed label and ignores new input
options.misconception: assumes perception is memory retrieval only

questions.explanation: Colour constancy arises from relational comparison with the surround, not from a fixed label. The tempting idea that the eye simply relabels the surface misses this comparison.
questions.hint: Think about the surround, not the surface alone.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Why Opponent Channels Appeal and What They Leave Open
questions.learningObjective: Identify a limit of opponent-process colour theory

stimulus.body: An amateur astronomer logs a red-green afterimage and a blue-yellow afterimage. Opponent channels explain the pairs well, yet some hues sit between the named pairs.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures what opponent channels explain and what they leave open?

options.text: They explain every hue without exception
options.misconception: overstates the coverage of opponent channels

options.text: They explain paired afterimages but not all intermediate hues
They replace trichromatic theory entirely
options.misconception: treats the two theories as mutually exclusive

options.text: They describe only brightness, not colour
options.misconception: confuses opponent channels with luminance coding

questions.explanation: Opponent channels account for paired afterimages but leave intermediate hues open. The claim that they replace trichromatic theory confuses complementary accounts.
questions.hint: Opponent pairs are not the whole story.

questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Table of Sound Intensities
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of sound intensities and compare levels
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer records 60 dB at the observatory gate and 90 dB near the generator; how many times greater is the intensity at the generator?

options.text: 3 times greater because the difference is 30 dB
options.misconception: treats decibels as a linear intensity scale

options.text: 10 times greater because each 10 dB is one decade
options.misconception: miscounts the number of ten-decibel steps

options.text: 30 times greater by direct subtraction of the values
options.misconception: subtracts decibel values as if they were intensities

options.text: 1000 times greater because 30 dB equals three ten-decibel steps

questions.explanation: A 30 dB difference means 10 cubed, or 1000, times the intensity. Linear subtraction or a single decade both misread the logarithmic scale.
questions.hint: Each 10 dB step multiplies intensity by 10.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Intensity Against Loudness
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish physical intensity from perceived loudness
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer notes the generator reads 90 dB yet seems only somewhat louder than the 60 dB gate; what explains the gap?

options.text: Perceived loudness follows a compressive function of intensity
Loudness grows linearly with decibels
options.misconception: assumes a linear relation between dB and loudness

options.text: The ear blocks high frequencies at night
options.misconception: invents a frequency block not in the scenario

options.text: The decibel meter is miscalibrated
options.misconception: blames the instrument instead of perception

questions.explanation: Perceived loudness is a compressive function of physical intensity, so equal dB steps feel unequal. Treating dB as loudness or blaming the meter misses this.
questions.hint: Loudness is not the same as intensity.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a constancy claim
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer claims a red star looks red at noon and midnight because memory fixes the label; is this full account?

options.text: Yes, because memory dominates colour naming
No, because constancy needs surround comparison, not memory alone
No, because colour constancy never occurs at night
options.misconception: wrongly limits constancy by time of day

options.text: Yes, because the star's wavelength is fixed

questions.explanation: Colour constancy relies on surround comparison and illuminant discounting, not memory alone. Wavelength fixity does not explain perception.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Why Opponent Channels Appeal and What They Leave Open
questions.learningObjective: Explain opponent-channel afterimages
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer asks why staring at blue yields a yellow afterimage; what mechanism explains it?

answer.exemplar: Staring at blue fatigues the blue response in the blue-yellow opponent channel, so when the stimulus is removed the channel swings toward yellow, producing the afterimage.

questions.explanation: Fatigue in one side of an opponent channel swings the response to the other side. This explains the afterimage colour.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Table of Sound Intensities
questions.learningObjective: Compute an intensity ratio from dB
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's table shows 40 dB, 60 dB, and 80 dB; which value is 100 times the 40 dB intensity?

options.text: 40 dB, because it is the reference
80 dB, because the difference is 40 dB
60 dB, because the difference is 20 dB
None, because dB cannot be multiplied

questions.explanation: A 20 dB difference gives an intensity ratio of 100. The 40 dB and 60 dB values differ by 20 dB.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Intensity Against Loudness
questions.learningObjective: Apply compressive loudness to a comparison
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer compares a 50 dB tone with a 70 dB tone; which sounds louder and is it ten times louder?

options.text: They sound the same because both are mid-range
The 70 dB tone sounds ten times louder
options.misconception: treats the dB step as a loudness multiplier

options.text: The 50 dB tone sounds louder
The 70 dB tone sounds louder but not ten times louder

questions.explanation: The 70 dB tone is louder, but loudness is compressive, so it is not ten times louder. Linear multiplier and reversal both fail.
questions.hint: Loudness is not linear in dB.

questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Hearing One Band of Pitches
questions.learningObjective: Identify the least sensitive band
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer asks which pitches need the greatest intensity to be heard; which band is least sensitive?

options.text: The mid-high band near 3000 Hz
options.misconception: confuses peak sensitivity with least sensitivity

options.text: The highest audible frequencies, near 20000 Hz
The deep bass near 50 Hz
options.misconception: picks low rather than high extremes

options.text: All bands need equal intensity

questions.explanation: The highest audible frequencies need the greatest intensity. The mid-high band is most sensitive, and extremes differ.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Two-Hertz Change in Pitch
questions.learningObjective: Judge relative detectability of pitch changes
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer notices a 4 Hz change at 2000 Hz; is the same 4 Hz change easier or harder at 500 Hz?

options.text: The same, because the change is identical
Harder, because lower pitches are harder to hear
options.misconception: confuses pitch level with change detectability

options.text: Easier, because 4 Hz is a larger fraction of 500 Hz
Impossible, because 500 Hz is below threshold
options.misconception: invents a threshold for the base tone

questions.explanation: The same 4 Hz change is a larger fraction of 500 Hz, so it is easier to detect. Absolute and level-based reasoning both fail.
questions.hint: Compare the change to the base.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: The Sense That Reports Gravity and Head Movement
questions.learningObjective: Explain vestibular function
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer asks how the inner ear detects head tilt; what is the mechanism?

answer.exemplar: Hair cells in the vestibular organs bend with head movement and gravity, converting mechanical force into neural signals that report tilt and acceleration.

questions.explanation: Vestibular hair cells transduce mechanical force from head movement and gravity into neural signals. This is the basis of balance perception.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: From Light to a Reported Object
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise perceptual stages
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer sees a dim star, then names it; which sequence best captures the full process?

options.text: Perception, transduction, sensation, recognition
Recognition, perception, sensation, transduction
Sensation, recognition, transduction, perception
Transduction, sensation, perception, recognition

questions.explanation: Light is transduced into neural signals, sensed, perceived as an object, then recognised. Any other order breaks the process.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: Estimating a Threshold in a Two-Alternative Task
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a threshold method
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer uses a single yes-no trial at one brightness to claim a threshold; what is the flaw?

options.text: Yes-no trials are always invalid
One trial and one level cannot estimate a threshold reliably
Brightness is irrelevant to threshold
Thresholds require at least ten observers

questions.explanation: A single trial at one level cannot estimate threshold; multiple levels and trials are needed. Yes-no methods can work with enough data.

questions.topic: Sensation and Perception: A Colour That Keeps Its Name in Changing Light
questions.learningObjective: Apply colour constancy to a scene
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's red filter is viewed under green light; constancy predicts it still looks red?

options.text: Yes, because memory overrides the light
No, because green light always makes red look black
options.misconception: overstates the effect of the illuminant

options.text: Yes, if the surround comparison supports identity
No, because constancy fails for filters

questions.explanation: Constancy can preserve identity under coloured light if surround comparison supports it. Memory alone or blanket failure both misread the principle.

Red-blue and green-yellow pairs
Red-yellow and blue-green pairs
Red-green and blue-yellow pairs

questions.explanation: Opponent channels use red-green and blue-yellow pairs. Other pairings or omitting colour pairs misstate the theory.
questions.hint: Red pairs with green, blue with yellow.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a loudness claim
